extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of public relations, political communication, and crowd psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for designing and executing propaganda and crowd-manipulation efforts, including analysis of context, site selection, message preparation, authority, delivery, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: History suggests that the socioeconomic and political context and location influence dramatically the potential for crowd manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conducive time periods and political climates (examples given: prelude to American Revolution, Roaring Twenties, Great Depression, Cold War, Interwar Period, Post-World War II, collapse of the Soviet Union, 2008 U.S. presidential election). Conduct thorough audience analysis to understand desires, fears, concerns, and biases using scientific studies, focus groups, and polls. Historical context and events (e.g., 1968 Columbia protest, 1992 Poll Tax Protest, 1992 L.A. Riots) can increase the likelihood of unruly behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a crowd assembles provides opportunities to manipulate thoughts, feelings, and emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose location, weather conditions, lighting, sound, and the shape of the arena to influence participation. Use symbolic and tangible backdrops (examples: Brandenburg Gate, Ground Zero) to evoke emotions before speaking. Venue can amplify message (e.g., presidential addresses, iconic monuments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda and pre-propaganda (message preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-propaganda (sociological propaganda) prepares a target group to anticipate and receive the main message; direct propaganda must be preceded by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test messages in advance—Bernays: 'a message that is ineffective is worse than no message at all.' Ellul: sociological propaganda is slow, general, creates a climate of favorable preliminary attitudes (plowing before sowing). Sociological propaganda permeates culture via advertising, movies, education, and magazines to normalize a style of life and make direct propaganda effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority / prestige (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manipulator's credibility (ethos) and prestige contribute to persuasiveness and can paralyze critical faculties of the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate prestige via acquired prestige (titles, uniform) and personal prestige (inner strength, success). Maintain distance from the crowd to prevent scrutiny; prevent questioning of prestige because 'from the minute prestige is called into question, it ceases to be prestige.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery: visual, vocal, and verbal techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to sway a crowd depends on visual, vocal, and verbal delivery; effective rhetoric has specific stylistic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Churchill's 'Scaffolding of Rhetoric' essentials: correctness of diction (precise word choice), rhythm (long, rolling, sonorous sentences), accumulation of argument (rapid succession of waves of sound and vivid pictures), analogy (link unknown to familiar), and 'wild extravagance' (extreme expressions embodying feelings). Pay attention to body language, staging, and vocal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message targeting: appeal to emotions and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda should be addressed to the masses, aimed at emotions, and kept simple rather than many-sided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hitler's points summarized: address propaganda to the masses (not intellectuals), target emotions more than intellect, and avoid complex, many-sided messaging because mass receptivity is limited. Use simple, repeatable slogans and emotionally charged appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding crowd behavior — Classic theory (Le Bon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classic theory posits that crowds form a collective mind with new characteristics (submergence, contagion, suggestibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Bon's observed characteristics: (1) submergence/disappearance of conscious personality (mental unity), aided by anonymity and feelings of invincibility; (2) contagion—sentiments and acts spread and individuals sacrifice personal interest to collective interest; (3) suggestibility—crowd is hypnotically directed by a 'hypnotizer.' Use these dynamics when planning appeals that exploit anonymity, contagion, and suggestibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding crowd behavior — Modern theory and ESIM
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern critiques reject classic stereotyped views; crowds are heterogeneous, composed of small acquainted groups, and collective action depends on salient shared social identities (Elaborated Social Identity Model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for heterogeneity: participants seldom act in unison; crowds do not obliterate individual cognition. ESIM: collective action arises when a particular social identity becomes salient; policing and indiscriminate force can create redefined unity and escalate conflict. Avoid assuming uniform irrationality; plan based on salient identities and likely policing responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of crowd lifecycle (assembling, temporary gathering, dispersing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds typically undergo a beginning (assembling), middle (temporary gathering with varied participation), and ending (dispersal) phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembling often occurs via organized mobilization or impromptu word-of-mouth. During gathering, participation varies by event type (religious services see high participation). Dispersal moves participants to alternate locations. A 'riot' is defined as one or more individuals engaging in violence; empirical data: less than 10% of protest demonstrations involve violence (historical U.S./European data). Use lifecycle knowledge to time calls to action and exits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience analysis (research methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough audience analysis is essential to manipulate a crowd effectively by understanding desires, fears, concerns, and biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scientific studies, focus groups, and polls to uncover hidden motives and tailor messages; Bernays emphasized unlocking motives behind desires, not just stated reasons. Audience analysis informs pre-propaganda and message targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of influencers and opinion leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and contract those who most influence public opinion—key experts, celebrities, existing supporters, and interlacing groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bernays expedited influence by recruiting opinion leaders and celebrities to amplify and legitimize messages. Leverage existing social networks and high-prestige figures to seed ideas and create perceived consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical consideration / morality of manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethical use of crowd manipulation is debatable and depends on the manipulator's intention, means used, and ends achieved; techniques themselves can be philosophically neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between morally charged and neutral uses: some (Bernays) argued manipulation is necessary for order and division of labor; others warn of indoctrination and erosion of responsibility. Evaluate legitimacy based on transparency, goals, and consequences; recognize arguments that political technology is philosophically neutral and that being 'right' is insufficient without effective organization and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning and technique (integrative checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective crowd manipulation planning integrates multiple elements: context analysis, site selection, propaganda/pre-propaganda, authority, and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the campaign as sequential and interdependent: analyze context and audience, choose site, prepare the cultural climate via sociological propaganda, recruit authority figures/influencers, craft and pre-test simple emotional messages, and deliver them with skilled visual/vocal/verbal technique while anticipating policing and crowd identity dynamics.
